calories_portions_1.title: What a Calorie Means
calories_portions_1.description: Start with the simple idea behind calories.

q1.explanation: Calories describe energy. Your body uses that energy for breathing, moving, digesting, and more.

q2.prompt: Which statement about daily calorie needs is most accurate?

choices.b: Calorie needs only depend on height
choices.c: Calorie needs vary from person to person
choices.d: Only athletes need to think about calories

q2.explanation: Age, body size, activity, goals, and routine all affect calorie needs. There is no one perfect number for everyone.

q3.prompt: Which drinks provide little to no calories in their plain form?
q3.explanation: Plain water and black coffee are very low in calories. Oils and sugary drinks add much more energy.

q4.prompt: A food with more calories is always unhealthy.
q4.explanation: Higher-calorie foods can still be nutritious. Nuts, salmon, yogurt, and avocado all bring useful nutrients along with calories.

q5.prompt: Why can your calorie needs change over time?

choices.d: Activity, body size, and goals can all shift your needs

q5.explanation: Your routine is not static, so your energy needs are not static either.

calories_portions_2.title: Portions and Energy Density
calories_portions_2.description: See how volume and calorie density work together.

q1.prompt: What does it mean when a food is energy dense?

choices.b: It packs many calories into a small amount
choices.c: It is always high in protein

q1.explanation: Energy-dense foods can add up quickly because you do not need much volume to get a lot of calories.

q2.prompt: Which plate habit can help lower calories while keeping meals satisfying?

choices.a: Fill half the plate with vegetables

q2.explanation: Vegetables add volume and fiber, which can help meals feel bigger without adding many calories.

q3.prompt: Which changes usually lower calories without making a meal feel tiny?

choices.b: Use a smaller bowl or plate
choices.c: Add fruit or vegetables for volume

q3.explanation: Portion cues and higher-volume foods make it easier to keep meals satisfying.

q4.prompt: Why are liquid calories easy to overlook?

choices.d: Drinks can add energy without much fullness

q4.explanation: Sugary coffees, juices, and sodas can add a lot of energy while barely changing fullness.

q5.prompt: What is a helpful pause before getting seconds?

choices.a: Ask if dessert is available first
choices.b: Count how many bites you took
choices.c: Check whether you are still hungry or just eating automatically

q5.explanation: A short pause helps you notice fullness instead of eating on autopilot.

calories_portions_3.title: Build a Lighter Plate
calories_portions_3.description: Use satisfaction, not restriction, to shape meals.

q1.prompt: Which nutrients often help a meal feel more filling?
q1.explanation: Protein and fiber often improve fullness, which can make a meal more satisfying.

q2.prompt: Which snack is more likely to keep you full for longer?
q2.explanation: Protein plus fiber-rich fruit usually keeps you satisfied longer than a mostly refined snack.

q3.prompt: Which lunch upgrades can make a meal lighter but still satisfying?

choices.a: Choose grilled protein instead of fried

q3.explanation: Grilled protein and produce often improve fullness and lower the meal's calorie load.

q4.prompt: What is true about restaurant servings?

choices.d: They can be much larger than one serving

q4.explanation: Restaurant portions often exceed one serving, which is why splitting or saving part can help.

q5.prompt: Which snack pattern is usually more balanced?
q5.explanation: Combining carbs with protein or healthy fat usually makes a snack steadier and more filling.

calories_portions_4.title: Portion Awareness in Real Life
calories_portions_4.description: Use repeatable cues instead of trying to be perfect.

q1.prompt: Which habit makes portions easier to repeat consistently?

choices.c: Wait until you are overly hungry
choices.d: Use the same bowl, plate, or hand cue often

q1.explanation: Consistent cues reduce guesswork and make portion habits easier to repeat.

q2.prompt: If you want to snack from a large bag, what is a helpful first step?

choices.a: Eat directly from the bag while distracted
choices.b: Pour some into a bowl first

q2.explanation: A bowl gives you a visible stopping point and makes mindless eating less likely.

q3.prompt: Which habits support better portion awareness?

choices.c: Keep every snack package open nearby
choices.d: Slow down enough to notice fullness

q3.explanation: Serving cues and slower eating both make it easier to notice how much you actually want.

q4.prompt: Which mindset is most helpful after a larger meal?

choices.b: Skip food for the rest of the day
choices.c: Return to normal balanced choices at the next meal

q4.explanation: A single larger meal does not define your progress. Your overall pattern matters more.

q5.prompt: If you still feel hungry after a balanced meal, what is a useful first move?

choices.a: Add more high-volume foods like vegetables or fruit first
choices.b: Assume you should never eat more

q5.explanation: High-volume foods can add satisfaction while keeping the meal balanced.

macro_basics_1.title: Meet the Macros
macro_basics_1.description: Get the big picture on protein, carbs, and fats.

q1.prompt: Which macro is especially important for building and repairing body tissue?
q1.explanation: Protein supports repair, recovery, and many important body functions.

q2.prompt: Which macro is the body's easiest energy source for many daily activities?
q2.explanation: Carbohydrates are a major fuel source for your brain, muscles, and everyday movement.

q3.prompt: Which macros provide 4 calories per gram?
q3.explanation: Protein and carbs provide 4 calories per gram. Fat provides 9 calories per gram.

q4.prompt: Why does your body still need some fat?

choices.a: Fat helps with hormones, cells, and vitamin absorption

q4.explanation: Fat supports many important functions, including absorption of vitamins A, D, E, and K.

q5.prompt: What is the healthiest way to think about macros?

choices.a: One macro should always be zero
choices.c: Carbs and fats are always bad
choices.d: Each macro has a role in a balanced pattern

q5.explanation: Balanced eating is usually about proportions and quality, not treating one macro as the enemy.

macro_basics_2.title: Protein Basics
macro_basics_2.description: Learn why protein matters and where to find it.

q1.prompt: Why is it helpful to include protein across the day instead of only at dinner?

choices.a: It can support fullness and recovery throughout the day

q1.explanation: Spreading protein across meals can make eating more satisfying and support muscle repair.

q2.prompt: Which snack is a stronger protein choice?
q2.explanation: Greek yogurt is a classic higher-protein snack compared with sweets or drinks.

q3.prompt: Which foods are good protein sources?
q3.explanation: Tofu and salmon both provide meaningful protein.

q4.prompt: What is true about a very high-protein eating pattern?

choices.a: It means vegetables no longer matter
choices.b: It automatically fixes every nutrition problem
choices.c: You still need carbs, fats, and produce too

q4.explanation: Protein matters, but a healthy pattern still includes a range of foods.

q5.prompt: After strength training, which meal pattern is helpful?

choices.b: Include a meal or snack with protein

q5.explanation: A protein-containing meal or snack can support recovery after lifting or resistance work.

macro_basics_3.title: Carbs and Fiber
macro_basics_3.description: Separate helpful carb habits from carb fear.

q1.explanation: Fiber is a kind of carbohydrate that supports fullness, digestion, and overall health.

q2.prompt: Which foods often provide both carbs and fiber?
q2.explanation: Beans, fruit, vegetables, and whole grains are common fiber-rich carb foods.

q3.prompt: Which choices are usually higher-fiber carb options?
q3.explanation: Oats and beans usually bring more fiber than sugary drinks or candy.

q4.prompt: Why pair carbs with protein or fat in a snack?

choices.b: To make the snack more filling and steady
choices.c: Because carbs should never be eaten alone

q4.explanation: Adding protein or fat can help slow the meal down and improve staying power.

q5.prompt: What is a balanced view of carbohydrates?

choices.c: They can support energy, exercise, and everyday life
choices.d: They should never appear at dinner

q5.explanation: Carbs can be very useful. Quality and context matter more than fear.

macro_basics_4.title: Better Fat Choices
macro_basics_4.description: See why fat quality and portions both matter.

q1.prompt: Which type of fat is generally considered the heart-friendlier choice?
q1.explanation: Unsaturated fats, like those in nuts, seeds, olive oil, and fish, are often the better choice.

q2.prompt: Which food pair contains mostly unsaturated fats?
q2.explanation: Olive oil and nuts are classic examples of foods rich in unsaturated fat.

q3.prompt: Which foods are known for helpful fats?
q3.explanation: Salmon and avocado bring fats that can fit well in a balanced diet.

q4.prompt: How can fat improve a meal?

choices.a: It adds flavor and can help meals feel satisfying
choices.d: It means fiber no longer matters

q4.explanation: Fat adds flavor and satisfaction, which is one reason balanced meals feel better than ultra-low-fat meals.

q5.prompt: Why do portions still matter with healthy fats?

choices.c: Healthy fats do not count if they are natural
choices.d: Even healthy fats are calorie dense

q5.explanation: Healthy fats are valuable, but they are still energy dense, so portions matter.

balanced_meals_labels_1.title: Build a Balanced Plate
balanced_meals_labels_1.description: Use a simple meal pattern you can repeat anywhere.

q1.explanation: A balanced plate often includes protein, a carb source, and produce.

q2.prompt: About how much of a plate can vegetables or fruit take up in a balanced meal?

choices.d: Around half the plate is a helpful target

q2.explanation: Half a plate of produce is a practical visual cue, not a strict rule.

q3.prompt: Which breakfast pieces help make a meal more balanced?
q3.explanation: Protein plus fruit or another fiber source makes breakfast feel more complete.

q4.prompt: How could you make instant noodles more balanced?

choices.b: Only eat half and stay hungry
choices.c: Add vegetables and a protein source

q4.explanation: Adding protein and vegetables makes a quick meal more complete.

q5.prompt: What is true about balanced meals?

choices.a: They must look identical every day
choices.b: They can look different while following the same pattern

q5.explanation: Balanced eating is a pattern, not one exact plate.

balanced_meals_labels_2.title: Read the Label
balanced_meals_labels_2.description: Use the serving size and numbers to compare foods wisely.

q1.prompt: The nutrition label is based on which amount?

choices.c: The serving size listed on the label

q1.explanation: Serving size is the reference point for the calories and nutrients on the label.

q2.prompt: If you eat two servings, what usually happens to the calories and macros?
q2.explanation: Two servings usually means about twice the calories and nutrients shown per serving.

q3.prompt: Which label numbers can help you compare two similar packaged foods?
q3.explanation: Added sugar and protein can both be useful comparison points, depending on the food.

q4.prompt: What does it usually mean if an ingredient appears first on the list?

choices.b: There is more of it by weight than the ingredients after it

q4.explanation: Ingredients are usually listed in descending order by weight.

q5.prompt: What is the healthiest way to use food labels?

choices.c: Only when a doctor forces you
choices.d: As a tool to compare options and notice patterns

q5.explanation: Labels are practical tools. They help with choices, not food guilt.

balanced_meals_labels_3.title: Healthy Swaps That Stick
balanced_meals_labels_3.description: Choose swaps you can actually repeat, not ones you will resent.

q1.prompt: Which drink swap is often a simple way to lower sugar?

choices.d: Choose water or unsweetened tea instead of soda

q1.explanation: Drink swaps are powerful because liquid sugar can add up fast.

q2.prompt: Which lunch choice is usually the lighter swap?
q2.explanation: Grilled protein and vegetables usually make a lighter, more balanced lunch.

choices.b: Choose whole grain bread instead of white when you enjoy it
choices.c: Replace every meal with only salad forever
choices.d: Swap chips for fruit and nuts sometimes

q3.explanation: Realistic swaps work because you can repeat them, not because they are extreme.

q4.prompt: What makes a healthy swap more likely to last?

choices.a: It still feels satisfying and practical
choices.b: It is the most restrictive option possible

q4.explanation: If the swap still tastes good and fits your life, it is easier to keep.

choices.a: They do not matter at all
choices.c: Repeated small choices can add up over time

q5.explanation: Consistency beats drama. Small repeatable changes often create the biggest long-term shift.

balanced_meals_labels_4.title: Everyday Nutrition Decisions
balanced_meals_labels_4.description: Bring the basics into busy days and imperfect situations.

q1.prompt: If lunch was low in protein, what is a smart next move?

choices.b: Add protein to your next meal or snack
choices.d: Assume the whole day is ruined

q1.explanation: Nutrition choices work together across the day, so the next meal is always another chance.

q2.prompt: After a heavier dinner than planned, what is the best next step?

choices.a: Punish yourself with an extreme fast
choices.c: Return to your normal balanced pattern at the next meal

q2.explanation: A heavier meal does not need a dramatic fix. Calm consistency works better.

q3.prompt: Which convenience-store choices can make a stronger quick snack?
q3.explanation: Yogurt plus fruit is a quick combo with protein, carbs, and more staying power.

q4.prompt: What can influence hunger besides food choice?

choices.b: Only the color of your plate

q4.explanation: Hunger is shaped by more than meals. Sleep, stress, and hydration all play a role.

q5.prompt: If you crash every afternoon, what is a useful first question?

choices.a: Did lunch include enough food, protein, or fiber?
choices.c: Do I need candy every hour?

q5.explanation: Afternoon energy often improves when earlier meals are more balanced and satisfying.
